question: Recent reports of the practice of grindadráp in the Faroe Islands, where hundreds of pilot whales and dolphins are killed each year, are causing serious concerns. On average, 600–700 deaths are estimated annually, while 2021 saw the largest recorded killing of over 1 400 animals in one day. For 2025, international organisations report almost 1 000 killings.

Pilot whales are highly social and extremely intelligent marine mammals, and their systematic slaughter affects the structure and balance of the North Atlantic marine ecosystem. At the same time, scientific research has shown that their meat contains high levels of mercury and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), which pose serious risks to public health.

Although the Faroe Islands are not a member of the EU, they benefit from European agreements and partnerships through Denmark, without making corresponding commitments to the protection of marine mammals. Accordingly: 1.
How does the Commission assess these practices in relation to the EU's principles of protection of marine species and biodiversity?
Will the Commission consider linking European agreements and funding to clauses on the protection of marine mammals?
Will the Commission undertake international initiatives to strengthen the protection of pilot whales and dolphins?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.2.2026) The Commission attaches great importance to the protection of marine biodiversity and to the conservation of cetaceans, as reflected in EU legislation prohibiting the deliberate capture or killing of such species in EU waters1 and the placing on the market of derived products2.

Under Article 355(5) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU, EU law does not apply to the Faroe Islands. Nevertheless, the Commission considers that the protection of marine species is a shared international responsibility and continues to promote high conservation standards in its external relations. The Commission recalls that cooperation with the Faroe Islands is based on separate bilateral agreements.

The Commission raises concerns related to cetacean conservation with the Faroese authorities in annual consultation meetings held under the Memorandum of Understanding on enhanced cooperation3. These exchanges provide an opportunity to promote dialogue, transparency and alignment with internationally recognised conservation standards.

At international level, the Commission supports multilateral efforts to improve the conservation of cetaceans, including through relevant international conventions and regional cooperation fora. It will continue to engage with partners, including Denmark and the Faroe Islands, to encourage dialogue, scientific cooperation and alignment with internationally recognised standards for the protection of all cetaceans.
1 Habitats Directive, Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of

wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, p. 7–50. 2 EU Wildlife Trade Regulation, Council Regulation (EC) No 338/97 of 9 December 1996 on the protection of species of wild fauna and flora by regulating trade therein, OJ L 61, 3.3.1997, p. 1–69. 3 https://www.eeas.europa.eu/sites/default/files/documents/2024/20240321%20Signed%20MoU.pdf.
